Summary: The dual attack is one of the main strategies for attacking the learning-with-errors (LWE) problem. A recent line of work aims at provable analyses of dual attacks that rely on as few heuristic assumptions as possible.
We present a provable dual attack that recovers a subvector $\boldsymbol{s}_{\mathrm{guess}}$ of the LWE secret, and we derive an explicit lower bound on its success probability without any heuristic assumption. Our analysis unifies the provable approaches of Pouly and Shen (EUROCRYPT 2024) and Bashiri and Wiemers (J. Math. Cryptol. 2025), and removes the very few informal assumptions left in the previous works. Inspired by Qu, Tian, Wang, and Xu (ePrint 2026/2117), the dual vectors are sampled from the sublattice spanned by the first vectors of a reduced basis. Our key ingredient is a first-moment estimate for the wrong candidates, which is based on the exact uniform distribution of some appearing cosets. This leads us to discard certain typical assumptions on shortest vectors from previous works.
We apply our results to ML-KEM, under one heuristic on its structured matrix, and improve on the first provable dual attack by $22$ to $52$ bits without any assumption on the rank of the sublattice, and by $47$ to $100$ bits ($21$ to $56$ bits compared with Qu, Tian, Wang, and Xu (ePrint 2026/2117)) if this rank is bounded as in Qu, Tian, Wang, and Xu (ePrint 2026/2117). We also apply our results to ML-DSA, and demonstrate the attack experimentally on small instances.
Our results do not threaten the security of ML-KEM or ML-DSA.

item.title: Regular Syndrome Decoding Is Easier Than Previously Estimated
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2563
Authors: Jiseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Changmin Lee, Hochang Lee
Summary: The Regular Syndrome Decoding (RSD) problem is a structured variant of classical Syndrome Decoding and underlies a growing number of efficient cryptographic constructions, including zero-knowledge protocols, pseudorandom correlation generators, and MPC-in-the-Head signatures. Although RSD is generally believed to be computationally hard, recent works have shown that algebraic attacks can outperform information-set decoding on important RSD parameter regimes.
Building on this line of work, we revisit the concrete hardness of RSD and show that many widely used parameter sets are substantially easier to solve than previously estimated. This improvement stems from a refined hybrid-algebraic attack that exposes and removes a previously overlooked source of concrete complexity: the joint blockwise placement of zero-coordinate guesses and syndrome-based variable eliminations. Rather than treating the two guessing stages and linear elimination as largely separate choices, our method coordinates them across all regular blocks so that the guessing penalty is balanced while sufficient equations are retained for linearization. This gives a systematic block-balancing principle for the entire guess–reduce–solve pipeline.
We reassess several RSD-based applications, including Ferret (CCS~2020), Wolverine (IEEE S\&P~2021), and committed VOLE (CCS~2025). Our estimates place at least one parameter set per application below its 128-bit target, with losses approaching 67~bits. On PCG benchmarks, we improve previous best attack costs by up to 29.77 and 25.91~bits over non-binary and binary fields, respectively. Moreover, for the revised 128-bit PCG parameter sets of Liu et al. (EUROCRYPT~2024) evaluated here, estimated attack costs are all below $2^{111}$ field operations. These results substantially revise the concrete-security landscape of RSD and indicate that several existing parameter choices overestimate the hardness of their underlying RSD instances.

item.title: A New Approach to Reducing Modulus Requirements in Homomorphic Computation: Precision Allocation in CKKS
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2562
Authors: Zhaoyang Liang, Runkun Liu, Jingwei Fang, Dan Ding
Summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation over encrypted data subject to the prescribed security and precision requirements (allowable deviations from ideal results). Among all FHE schemes, CKKS is a representative scheme for approximate arithmetic, allowing the same operation on multiple values packed into a single RLWE ciphertext.
Reducing ciphertext modulus \(Q\) for given output precision requirements under RLWE security constraints is a central challenge in homomorphic computation. However, despite advances in plaintext and ciphertext representations, algorithmic optimizations, and modulus management, the budget in most existing approaches remains dependent on the highest required precision and cannot reduce the baseline modulus cost to overcome encryption noise.
In this work, we make average rather than maximum precision requirements govern the modulus budget and achieve savings in the baseline cost. Under decryption correctness constraints, we make these possible by allocating arbitrary output precision among independent values and quantify the modulus savings arising from differences in their precision requirements.
As a bonus, our construction preserves the standard CKKS ciphertext format, which helps maintain compatibility with existing optimizations. And the construction inherits the IND-CPA security of CKKS without additional cryptographic assumptions.
With a 64-bit average precision requirement, we transfer 75 bits of precision without reducing evaluation depth and up to 735 bits while preserving correct initial recovery, raising the precision allocated to the target values to 2,269 bits. For six successive squarings of 256 messages targeting 224-bit precision, our implementation reduces the initial modulus bit length by 67\% compared with standard CKKS, allowing a fourfold reduction in ring dimension.

item.title: SALUS: Large-Scale Homomorphic Circuit Synthesis via Logic-Aware LUT Optimization
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2561
Authors: Ran Mao, Zhou Zhang, Zian Zhao, Zhenyu Guan, Peng Yin, Song Bian
Summary: Recently, growing interests are developed in optimizing fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) circuits to enable Boolean function evaluations over ciphertexts. While existing works utilize functional bootstrapping (FBS) to efficiently evaluate logic gates, the evaluation efficiency for large-scale circuits remains limited. Recent advances introduce a fast ciphertext conversion method, making it feasible to evaluate look-up tables (LUTs) over homomorphic multiplexer operation. In this work, we propose a new circuit synthesis framework, SALUS, which automatically generates and evaluates gate-level graphs over homomorphic LUTs given an input Boolean circuit. We apply the binary decision diagram (BDD) reordering method and multi-value refresh techniques to efficiently evaluate complex LUTs. Additionally, we propose a heuristic algorithm to merge LUTs in a given circuit into multi-output LUTs. In the experiments, we examine the efficiency of SALUS using a wide range of benchmark suites, including the EPFL and ISCAS benchmark circuits. We show that SALUS achieves a maximum reduction of up to 26× in computational latency compared to state-of-the-art homomorphic circuit synthesis method. Furthermore, we evaluate real-world applications, e.g., image filtering and matrix multiplication, and achieve an average speedup of 8.6× (with a maximum speedup of 24×) compared to the FBS-based method.

item.title: Graphs and cycles in curve-based collision walks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2560
Authors: Sebastiano Boscardin, Jolijn Cottaar, Monika Trimoska
Summary: In this work, we look at collision-based attacks both for elliptic curve and isogeny problems. Our main focus is on attacks in the multi-user setting, i.e., where one tries to recover all secret keys of a large set of $L$ public keys simultaneously, in a faster way than the total time required to attack each key individually. We consider three different problems: (1) the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves, (2) the isogeny pathfinding problem on supersingular $\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$-curves, (3) the isogeny pathfinding problem on supersingular $\mathbb{F}_p$-curves. We first survey the existing van Oorschot and Wiener style attacks on these three problems. Then we propose versions of the pseudorandom walks that are better suited for isogeny pathfinding problems without additional restrictions. We then apply these new walks to the multi-user setting and analyse which properties we can achieve compared to the discrete logarithm case where we show that we can extract all $L$ public keys with $L$ useful collisions and without an infiltrator (a user for which we know the secret key). Specifically, for (2) we can extract $L$ public keys with approximately $L + \log(L)$ useful collisions and no infiltrator needed. Our analysis shows however that heuristic and infiltrator-aided strategies are more efficient while enjoying practically similar gains. For (3) we can extract approximately $0.75L$ public keys with $L$ useful collisions, but with an infiltrator.

item.title: FN-DSA on Arm Cortex-M55: Revisiting a Floating-Point Lattice Signature with Native FP64 and Helium
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2559
Authors: Seung-Won Lee, Min-Joo Sim, Min-Seo Kim, Hwa-Jeong Seo
Summary: FN-DSA has the shortest signatures among NIST's post-quantum signature standards, but on microcontrollers its signing is slow because the binary64 arithmetic it specifies is emulated with integer instructions. Previous speedups either change the arithmetic or the order of random sampling, so their signatures no longer match the known-answer tests (KATs) of the reference implementation, or rely on double-precision SIMD instructions that microcontrollers lack. The Arm Cortex-M55 has both a double-precision FPU and the M-Profile Vector Extension (MVE). On this core, we present the first FN-DSA implementation that, unlike these approaches, reproduces the KATs of the reference and runs in constant time, yet is faster than the reference. On MVE, we vectorize the NTTs with layer merging and the fixed-point FFT of key generation with split-word Q32 arithmetic on 32-bit lanes. On the FPU, bit-exact FP64 computes the FFT, LDL decomposition, split, merge and sampler of signing without changing any result, and exponent-normalized division turns the bit-by-bit divisions of key generation into a single VDIV.F64 with operand-independent latency. For Keccak, vectorized bit interleaving speeds up every permutation, and request-level batching processes four independent verification requests at once; SLOTHY then reschedules our MVE and Keccak assembly. Key generation, signing and verification become up to 1.23x, 1.93x and 1.30x faster than the reference on the same core, and batch verification of four signatures up to 1.75x faster. Overall, the FPU pays off where the reference emulates an operation with many integer instructions, and MVE where it already computes with integers or fixed point.

item.title: Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2557
Authors: Olivier Gillot, William J. Buchanan, Madjid G. Tehrani
Summary: With Q-day approaching, the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has begun, with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards. This paper benchmarks the three NIST-standardised PQC algorithms—FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)—across key generation, signing and verification operations, measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL 3.5, results show that ML-KEM and ML-DSA achieve energy and speed efficiency comparable to classical elliptic-curve cryptography across all tested architectures. However, SLH-DSA signing is inadvisable on constrained hardware: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware, making it impractical for resource-limited IoT deployments. These findings have direct implications for IoT security practitioners planning PQC migration.

item.title: Registered ABE via Predicate Encodings, Revisited
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2558
Authors: Junichi Tomida
Summary: Predicate encodings, proposed by Wee (TCC'14), are a simple framework that abstracts a variety of attribute-based encryption (ABE) schemes. Zhu et al. showed how to apply predicate encodings to registered ABE (Reg-ABE) using the same definition as in vanilla ABE (Asiacrypt'23). We provide a new definition of predicate encodings that is more suitable for registered ABE and allows us to obtain more efficient Reg-ABE schemes than those by Zhu et al. for predicates captured by predicate encodings. Notably, we obtain \begin{itemize} \item the first Reg-ABE scheme for (non-)zero inner product with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \item the first Reg-ABE scheme for conjunctions/disjunctions with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \item the first registered broadcast encryption scheme with $ O(\log L) $-size ciphertexts, \end{itemize} under the standard $ k $-Lin assumption, where $ L $ denotes the maximum number of users. Prior to our work, Reg-ABE schemes for (non-)zero inner product, conjunctions, and disjunctions require $ O(\ell\log L) $-size ciphertexts where $ \ell $ is the vector length or the policy size, and registered broadcast encryption schemes rely on the generic group model.

item.title: Analysis of an AI based code distinguisher
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2556
Authors: Quentin Lavit, Julien Seinturier, Pascal Véron
Summary: Recently, DeepDistinguisher demonstrated the capability of transformer-like architectures to accurately distinguish Goppa codes from linear codes randomly generated, outperforming traditional distinguishers in certain settings. The purpose of our research is to examine the working mechanism of the mentioned machine learning algorithm. In particular, we explore the performance of the distinguisher using saliency maps and attention visualization techniques. We first identify a low-weight-row artifact present in the random instances used during training and show that the model partially relies on this feature. After removing this artifact, the distinguisher still achieves significant accuracy, suggesting the use of more structural properties. Inspired by the constraints induced by the minimum distance of Goppa codes, we proposed a rule based on pairwise XOR operation between the rows of the generator matrix. Our experiments have shown that the predictions made by DeepDistinguisher and XOR-based rule are highly correlated especially for high-rate codes. Furthermore, when evaluated on random matrices satisfying both the minimum distance and XOR constraints, the neural distinguisher loses most of its predictive power. This suggests that transformer-based architectures exploit general combinatorial properties of a code rather than some hidden underlying algebraic structure.

item.title: Post-quantum commutative group actions from oriented superspecial abelian varieties
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2555
Authors: Wouter Castryck, Bogdan Adrian Dina, Péter Kutas, Gioella Lorenzon
Summary: We study the cryptographic use of Shimura class group actions on superspecial principally polarized abelian varieties equipped with a CM orientation, within the context of post-quantum cryptography. Besides giving an accessible introduction to the topic, illustrated with many examples, we provide tools for representing CM orientations through higher-dimensional isogenies and for computing the Shimura class group action in the restricted effective group action model. Here, key auxiliary results are a version of Kani's lemma "with CM" and a trick that often allows to halve the ambient dimension. We also give a method for finding superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces that are oriented by a given CM order, which is extracted from an algebraic framework for studying CM orientations using the Ibukiyama-Katsura-Oort correspondence. We also analyze obstructions to transitivity of the Shimura class group action, related to the characteristic-zero notion of CM type.

item.title: Concrete LDVR Attacks with Fewer Signers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2554
Authors: Renas Bacho
Summary: We improve the concrete parameters of the attacks on the low-dimensional vector representation (LDVR) problem by Rodríguez García and Tessaro (ePrint 2026/2126), whose attack on canonical evaluation points uses $5{,}020$ signers. By combining their Chinese remainder theorem construction with a generalized birthday search over many challenges, we obtain a concrete attack with $488$ signers and $173$ corruptions over the Curve25519 scalar field. In $64$ batches of $2^{25}$ challenges, the search finds solutions for six distinct challenges. We compare the counts measured at each stage of the search with predictions from an explicit heuristic model. For adversarially chosen evaluation points, we build on the binary attacks of Rodríguez García and Tessaro and give a construction that attains the optimal LDVR success probability for every oracle query budget when $2\le n\le253$ and $t_c=t$ in the uniform oracle model. At $228$ signers and $114$ corruptions, our implementation finds a successful subset using SHA-512 challenges after a cumulative total of $360.13$ million queries across two runs, taking $168.60$ seconds in total. We also give an explicit set of $256$ evaluation points for which an efficient subset search attack using $128$ corruptions succeeds with probability at least $51.92\%$ per uniform challenge. For both canonical and adversarially chosen evaluation points, we analyze the query complexity and report measured and estimated running times.

item.title: Near-Optimal Early Stopping with Optimal Communication
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2553
Authors: Fatima Elsheimy, Simon Holmgaard Kamp, Julian Loss, Charalampos Papamanthou
Summary: Minimizing both the round and communication complexity of Byzantine agreement (BA) is a longstanding problem. In the synchronous setting, early stopping protocols aim to terminate in number of rounds that is proportional to the actual number $f\leq t$ of corruptions in an execution, rather than on the worst case threshold $t$. The lower bound on the round complexity for such protocols is known to be $\min\{f+2, t+1\}$ rounds. Existing protocols, however, achieve either round complexity close to the optimal bound or low communication complexity, but not both simultaneously. Elsheimy, Loss, and Papamanthou (ASIACRYPT 2024) obtain $(1+\epsilon)f+O(1)$ rounds for any $1> \epsilon>0$, with $O(n^4f \kappa)$ communication. In contrast, Lenzen and Sheikholeslami (PODC 2022) achieve asymptotically optimal $O(n \cdot t)$ communication for $t3$, but with a $25f+13$ number of rounds.
In this work, we present deterministic synchronous Byzantine agreement protocols that achieve new tradeoffs between early stopping round complexity and communication. For $t3$, without cryptographic setup, we obtain $f+O(\sqrt{f\log f})$ termination rounds with optimal $O(n\cdot t)$ communication (here and throughout, $\sqrt{f}$ denotes $\sqrt{f+1}$ and $\log f$ denotes $\log(f+2)$, so that the bounds are well defined when $f=0$). Thus, our round complexity has the optimal leading coefficient of one, with a sublinear additive overhead. By allowing slightly higher communication, we reduce this overhead to $O(\sqrt f)$, obtaining $f+O(\sqrt f)$ rounds with $O(n\cdot t+f^2\log f)$ communication. Finally, for $t<n/2$, assuming a public key infrastructure and threshold signatures, we obtain $f+O(\sqrt f)$ rounds with $O(n\cdot t\cdot\kappa)$ bits of communication, where $\kappa$ is the signature length.

item.title: CHARRM - Characterizing Hardware Leakage in the Robust Random Probing Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2552
Authors: Armand Schinkel, Pascal Sasdrich
Summary: Masking is a prevalent countermeasure against passive physical implementation attacks such as Side-Channel Analysis (SCA). Despite its theoretical soundness, the practical application of masking is often fraught with complexity and prone to errors, underscoring the necessity for automated security verification. This paper presents a comprehensive methodology for efficient security verification in the $(g, t, c)$-robust $(p, \epsilon)$-random probing model. In particular, we advance the state-of-the-art concept of leakage characteristics to account for robust probe extension schemes across arbitrary circuit structures, enabling efficient leakage probability bound computation for glitch-extended and transition-extended robust probing scenarios. By further linking the leakage characteristic to the Set of Input Shares (SIS) function, we extend our verification methodology to established composability notions. Our automated reasoning framework demonstrates practicality and superior performance and accuracy for larger circuits in comparative evaluations with \ironmask as state-of-the-art competitor. For the first time, our method allows for the exact verification of larger, composed circuit structures, validated by corresponding case studies. Consequently, this work advances the state-of-the-art in automated hardware security verification, providing a versatile tool for evaluating the security of masked cryptographic implementations against SCA in the presence of transient physical effects.

item.title: Privacy with Leakage from Falsifiable Assumptions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2551
Authors: Francesco Berti, Itamar Levi
Summary: An inherent challenge in cryptography is finding realistic and meaningful models and assumptions. Such assumptions must be fal- sifiable. For symmetric-key cryptography in the standard model (i.e., black-box without leakage), it is conjectured that we have identified the right assumptions: pseudorandom functions and permutations (PRFs and PRPs). However, when considering side-channel attacks (SCAs) that exploit physical side-channel leakage, the answer is less clear. Moreover, the requirements for integrity and privacy may differ in the leakage-aware SCA setting. For integrity: due to advances in the so-called unbounded leakage model, it is sufficient to claim integrity based only on black-box properties by instantiating a single strongly unpredictable-with-leakage (tweakable) block cipher. For privacy: one approach relied on simulatabil- ity, proposed by Yu and Standaert at CRYPTO 2013. That is, it should be possible to simulate leakage traces without access to the underlying secret key. Unfortunately, simulating the leakage behavior of a complex electronic system and arguing that distinguishing simulation from reality is hard has proved highly challenging (e.g., Galea et al., ASIACRYPT 2014, and Deperz et al., Cascade 2026). In this paper, we propose a new model and assumption. We isolate a key component, namely the key-refreshing process, and provide a security definition for it that is both falsifiable in practice and usable in security proofs: secure refreshing. Like simulatability, this assumption is designed to capture the security of the key-refreshing process. Rather than re- lying on a simulator, however, we formalize security through a direct refreshing experiment that can be practically falsified by evaluation lab- oratories. Therefore, our approach avoids many of the concrete problems and challenges associated with previous models. Furthermore, inspired by this new assumption (and its accompanying model), and to provide an additional security assumption for the strongly SCA-protected leak- free component, we introduce strongly protected secure refreshing. As one concrete example, using these assumptions, we prove the privacy of the well-known PSV encryption scheme. We provide the first privacy proof based only on falsifiable assumptions and, importantly, without assuming that the strongly protected component is leak-free which can effectively translate to significant computational cost reduction.
